The equilibrium temperature of a planet with albedo \(A\) is  

\[
T_{\text{eq}} = \left[\frac{(1-A)L_\star}{16\pi\sigma a^{2}}\right]^{1/4}
\]

so, for the same star and the same albedo,  

\[
T \propto a^{-1/2}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad a \propto T^{-2}.
\]

---

### 1.  Ratio of orbital distances  

\[
\frac{T_1}{T_2}=1.4,\qquad \frac{T_2}{T_3}=2.3
\]

\[
\frac{T_1}{T_3}=1.4\times2.3 = 3.22.
\]

Hence  

\[
\frac{a_3}{a_1}= \left(\frac{T_1}{T_3}\right)^{2}= (3.22)^{2}\approx 10.4 .
\]

Planet 3 orbits about 10.4 times farther from the star than Planet 1.

---

### 2.  Ratio of orbital periods  

Kepler’s third law (stellar mass dominates) gives  

\[
P^{2}\propto a^{3}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad P\propto a^{3/2}.
\]

Therefore  

\[
\frac{P_3}{P_1}= \left(\frac{a_3}{a_1}\right)^{3/2}= (10.4)^{3/2}
               = 10.4 \times \sqrt{10.4}
               \approx 10.4 \times 3.22
               \approx 33.4 .
\]

---

The mass ratios are not needed because the planets’ masses are negligible compared with the star’s mass in Kepler’s law.
